chapter.title: Structures de données – Vecteurs et Matrices

section.title: Introduction to Data Structures
section.content: Data structures allow data to be organized and stored in a structured manner to facilitate their manipulation. Until now, we have manipulated simple variables (integers, reals, booleans). But how do we store a list of 100 grades? Or a multiplication table? This is where vectors and matrices (also called arrays) come in.

bulletPoints.point: ▶️ A data structure is a container that groups several values together.
▶️ Vectors (1D arrays) store a sequence of elements of the same type.
▶️ Matrices (2D arrays) store data in the form of rows and columns.
▶️ They allow quick access to each element via its index.
💻 Example: a vector of 5 grades can be represented as grades = [12, 15, 8, 19, 10].

section.title: Vectors (One-Dimensional Arrays)
section.content: A vector is an ordered collection of elements of the same type, stored in contiguous memory cells. Each element is identified by its index (or position).

bulletPoints.point: 💻 Access to an element: grades[index]. Example: grades[3] = 14.
▶️ Indices generally start at 0 in programming.
▶️ Vector length: total number of elements.
💻 Example: Variables temp : Array[1..7] of Reals temp[1] ← 22.5 ; temp[2] ← 23.0 ; ...

section.title: Matrices (Two-Dimensional Arrays)
section.content: A matrix is a two-dimensional array, organized in rows and columns.

bulletPoints.point: 💻 Declaration: Variables mat : Array[1..L][1..C] of Integers
💻 Access: mat[row][column]. Example: mat[2][3].
▶️ Indices often start at 0 in programming.
🎯 Usefulness: grids, images, tabular data.
▶️ Example identity matrix: For i from 1 to 3 do For j from 1 to 3 do If i = j then identity[i][j] ← 1 Else identity[i][j] ← 0 EndFor EndFor.

section.title: Basic Operations on Vectors
section.content: Manipulating a vector often requires traversing its elements.

bulletPoints.point: ▶️ Traversal: For i from 1 to N do Process vector[i] EndFor.
▶️ Filling: For i from 1 to N do Read(vector[i]) EndFor.
▶️ Search: i ← 1 ; Found ← false While i <= N AND NOT Found do If vector[i] = value_sought then Found ← true i ← i + 1 EndWhile.
▶️ Sum / average: sum ← 0 For i from 1 to N do sum ← sum + vector[i] EndFor average ← sum / N.
▶️ Maximum: max ← vector[1] For i from 2 to N do If vector[i] > max then max ← vector[i] EndFor.
▶️ Traversal: For i from 1 to L do For j from 1 to C do Process mat[i][j] EndFor EndFor.
▶️ Filling: For i from 1 to L do For j from 1 to C do Read(mat[i][j]) EndFor EndFor.
▶️ Searching for a value in the entire matrix.
▶️ Sum: sum ← 0 For i from 1 to L do For j from 1 to C do sum ← sum + mat[i][j] EndFor EndFor.
▶️ Diagonals: main: mat[i][i] secondary: mat[i][C-i+1]
▶️ Addition: C[i][j] ← A[i][j] + B[i][j]
▶️ Multiplication: For i from 1 to L do For j from 1 to N do C[i][j] ← 0 For k from 1 to M do C[i][j] ← C[i][j] + A[i][k] * B[k][j] EndFor EndFor EndFor.
▶️ Transposition: Transposed[j][i] ← Mat[i][j]
▶️ Usage: graphics, AI, scientific computing.

section.title: Sorting Algorithms on Vectors
section.content: Sorting a vector is a fundamental operation.

bulletPoints.point: 🧠 Selection sort: For i from 1 to N-1 do minPos ← i For j from i+1 to N do If tab[j] < tab[minPos] then minPos ← j EndFor Swap tab[i] and tab[minPos] EndFor.
🧠 Bubble sort: Repeat swap ← false For i from 1 to N-1 do If tab[i] > tab[i+1] then Swap tab[i] and tab[i+1] swap ← true EndIf EndFor Until NOT swap.
❌ These sorts are simple but not very performant.
💻 Grade management: Read(n) For i from 1 to n do Read(grades[i]) EndFor sum ← 0 For i from 1 to n do sum ← sum + grades[i] EndFor average ← sum / n
💻 Matrix product: For i from 1 to L do For j from 1 to N do C[i][j] ← 0 For k from 1 to M do C[i][j] ← C[i][j] + A[i][k] * B[k][j] EndFor EndFor EndFor.

section.title: Best Practices and Tips
section.content: Best practices for vectors and matrices.

bulletPoints.point: ✔️ Choose the right size.
✔️ Use explicit names.
⚠️ Be careful with indices.
✔️ Check dimensions.
✔️ Factor out code.
